Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

KENNEDY SPACE CENTER, Florida (CNN) -- With space shuttle Atlantis on its way to upgrade the Hubble Space Telescope, that leaves one shuttle, Endeavour, at the ready on the other launch pad here. Space shuttle Endeavour, in background, sits poised to launch in case Atlantis, in foreground, meets trouble. And that's where everybody at NASA wants it to stay. "We have high confidence that we're just having that thing over on pad B to make it look nice," said mission flight director Tony Ceccaci. Endeavour is far more than a postcard picture -- it's on standby in case something goes seriously wrong with the Atlantis mission. For example, NASA has estimated there's a 1-in-221 chance the shuttle could be struck and crippled by orbiting space debris. If such an incident were to thrust the seven Atlantis astronauts into danger, Endeavour would blast off within days in a last-ditch attempt to save them. Endeavour Cmdr. Christopher Ferguson believes his crew is up to the task. "I feel as confident about our ability to pull this off, if need be, as I would any other mission," he said. The idea of a standby rescue spacecraft grew out of the 2003 Columbia disaster, in which that shuttle disintegrated over Texas during re-entry into the Earth's atmosphere. But until now, there's been no need. All the previous missions since Columbia have gone to the International Space Station. The crew of a damaged shuttle could take refuge there for months if need be until another shuttle was readied to retrieve them. But Atlantis is going to Hubble, whose orbit isn't anywhere near the space station. If their spacecraft malfunctioned, the seven-member Atlantis crew would have to survive aboard -- probably for days -- until they could be rescued. "In this case it's a much shorter fuse," Ferguson said. "Consumables like food and oxygen would run out quickly. So the reason we've gotten this crew trained and spooled up and ready to go on literally a moment's notice is because they [Atlantis's crew] have no place comfortable to go stay for a long period of time." But the rescue would be no cakewalk. Endeavour would need to pull up underneath Atlantis and hook on to the other shuttle using its robotic arm. Over the course of two days, the seven Atlantis astronauts would spacewalk over to Endeavour by holding on to a tether line strung between the two spaceships. Atlantis mission specialist John Grunsfeld would go first -- and, actually, twice. Grunsfeld would spacewalk to Endeavour, grab an extra EMU (extravehicular mobility unit) spacesuit and take it back to Atlantis. He would then return to Endeavour with one of the Atlantis astronauts not trained in spacewalking. With the Atlantis crew safely aboard, Endeavour would pull away and begin preparing to head home. Atlantis Cmdr. Scott Altman said that knowing Ferguson and the other three members of the Endeavour crew are ready in case of an emergency gives him peace of mind. "Even in the worst-possible imaginable case, we can stay up there and last until somebody comes up and gets us," Altman said. "So it feels like we have all our bases covered." So what would happen to Atlantis? Ferguson said mission leaders would prepare the crippled shuttle for what they call a "disposal burn" -- a safe, remotely controlled landing of Atlantis. "If it comes to it, we certainly don't want a space shuttle coming in over a populated area," he said. "So we want to control the burn so it does end up in the ocean." In all, eleven astronauts would be stuffed into Endeavour. A space shuttle has never carried that many. The four Endeavour crew members would hang out in the flight deck, while the seven Atlantis astronauts would squeeze into the mid-deck area. The journey back to Earth would be uncomfortable. But Ceccaci, the flight director, says that wouldn't matter as long as everyone was safe. "Wrap me in bubble wrap and get me home safely, I wouldn't care," he said. "I wouldn't care how cramped it is."

**KENNEDY SPACE CENTER, Florida (CNN) —** With space shuttle Atlantis on its way to upgrade the Hubble Space Telescope, one shuttle remains ready on the center’s other launch pad: Endeavour.

In the background, Endeavour sits poised to launch should Atlantis, visible in the foreground, encounter trouble. And that is exactly where everyone at NASA hopes it will remain.

“We have high confidence that we’re just having that thing over on pad B to make it look nice,” said mission flight director Tony Ceccaci.

But Endeavour is far more than a postcard image. It is on standby in case something goes seriously wrong with the Atlantis mission. NASA, for example, has estimated that there is a 1-in-221 chance the shuttle could be struck and crippled by orbiting space debris.

If such an incident were to endanger the seven Atlantis astronauts, Endeavour would launch within days in a last-ditch effort to rescue them.

Endeavour Cmdr. Christopher Ferguson believes his crew is equal to the task.

“I feel as confident about our ability to pull this off, if need be, as I would any other mission,” he said.

The concept of keeping a rescue spacecraft on standby emerged from the 2003 Columbia disaster, in which the shuttle disintegrated over Texas while re-entering Earth’s atmosphere. Until now, however, such a rescue craft has not been necessary.

Every shuttle mission since Columbia has traveled to the International Space Station, where the crew of a damaged shuttle could take refuge for months, if necessary, while another shuttle was prepared to retrieve them.

Atlantis, however, is headed to Hubble, whose orbit is nowhere near the space station. If their spacecraft malfunctioned, the seven-member Atlantis crew would have to survive aboard it—probably for days—until help arrived.

“In this case it’s a much shorter fuse,” Ferguson said. “Consumables like food and oxygen would run out quickly. So the reason we’ve gotten this crew trained and spooled up and ready to go on literally a moment’s notice is because they [Atlantis’s crew] have no place comfortable to go stay for a long period of time.”

The rescue would be no easy undertaking. Endeavour would have to maneuver beneath Atlantis and connect to the other shuttle using its robotic arm.

Over the course of two days, the seven Atlantis astronauts would spacewalk to Endeavour, holding on to a tether stretched between the two spacecraft.

Atlantis mission specialist John Grunsfeld would make the crossing first—and, in fact, twice. Grunsfeld would spacewalk to Endeavour, retrieve an extra EMU (extravehicular mobility unit) spacesuit and carry it back to Atlantis. He would then return to Endeavour accompanied by one of the Atlantis astronauts who had not been trained in spacewalking.

Once the Atlantis crew was safely aboard, Endeavour would pull away and begin preparing for the journey home.

Atlantis Cmdr. Scott Altman said that knowing Ferguson and the other three members of Endeavour’s crew were ready in the event of an emergency gave him peace of mind.

“Even in the worst-possible imaginable case, we can stay up there and last until somebody comes up and gets us,” Altman said. “So it feels like we have all our bases covered.”

What, then, would happen to Atlantis?

Ferguson said mission leaders would prepare the crippled shuttle for what they call a “disposal burn”—a safe, remotely controlled landing of Atlantis.

“If it comes to it, we certainly don’t want a space shuttle coming in over a populated area,” he said. “So we want to control the burn so it does end up in the ocean.”

In all, 11 astronauts would be packed into Endeavour—a number no space shuttle has ever carried. Endeavour’s four crew members would remain on the flight deck, while the seven Atlantis astronauts would squeeze into the mid-deck area.

The return to Earth would be uncomfortable. But Ceccaci, the flight director, said that would not matter as long as everyone made it home safely.

“Wrap me in bubble wrap and get me home safely, I wouldn’t care,” he said. “I wouldn’t care how cramped it is.”

Endeavour commander Christopher Ferguson said he trusts his crew’s ability to conduct such an operation as much as he would trust them on any other mission.

The plan to keep a rescue shuttle ready was developed after the 2003 Columbia tragedy, when the spacecraft broke apart over Texas while re-entering Earth’s atmosphere. No rescue mission has been necessary so far. Every post-Columbia flight before this one traveled to the International Space Station, where astronauts from a damaged shuttle could shelter for months while another vehicle was prepared to collect them.

Atlantis, however, is headed for Hubble, which follows an orbit far from the station. If Atlantis became unusable, its seven crew members would likely have to remain inside it for several days while waiting for help.

Ferguson explained that the limited supplies aboard would make the situation urgent. Food, oxygen and other necessities would be depleted rapidly, which is why his crew has been trained and placed on immediate alert. Unlike astronauts near the space station, the Atlantis crew would have no comfortable refuge where they could remain for an extended period.

The rescue itself would be extremely difficult. Endeavour would maneuver beneath Atlantis and use its robotic arm to attach itself to the disabled shuttle. During the next two days, all seven Atlantis astronauts would move between the spacecraft on spacewalks, gripping a tether stretched from one vehicle to the other.

Atlantis mission specialist John Grunsfeld would make the first crossing—and would complete the trip twice. He would initially travel to Endeavour, retrieve an additional EMU, or extravehicular mobility unit spacesuit, and carry it back to Atlantis. He would then cross to Endeavour again while accompanying an Atlantis astronaut who had not received spacewalk training.

After everyone from Atlantis was safely inside Endeavour, the rescue shuttle would separate and begin getting ready for its return to Earth.

Atlantis commander Scott Altman said he finds reassurance in knowing that Ferguson and Endeavour’s other three astronauts are prepared to respond. Even under the worst circumstances imaginable, Altman said, his crew could remain in orbit long enough for rescuers to reach them, making him feel that NASA had accounted for every possibility.

The damaged Atlantis would not be left drifting in space. Ferguson said mission managers would set it up for what NASA calls a “disposal burn,” remotely directing the shuttle toward a safe end. Because an uncontrolled re-entry could threaten populated areas, officials would guide Atlantis so that it came down in the ocean.

The rescue would place 11 astronauts aboard Endeavour, more people than any space shuttle has ever carried. Endeavour’s four-person crew would remain on the flight deck, while the seven rescued Atlantis astronauts crowded into the mid-deck.

The trip back would be cramped and unpleasant, but Ceccaci said comfort would be irrelevant if everyone returned safely. He added that he would accept being wrapped in bubble wrap and packed into a tight space as long as he made it home unharmed.

# Endeavour stands ready for rare shuttle rescue during Hubble mission

**CAPE CANAVERAL, Florida —** As space shuttle Atlantis races around Earth on a high-stakes mission to repair the Hubble Space Telescope, another shuttle is waiting on the launchpad for a mission NASA hopes it will never have to fly.

Space shuttle Endeavour has been prepared as the rescue vehicle for Atlantis and its seven astronauts during the final servicing mission to Hubble. The unusual precaution is necessary because Atlantis cannot reach the International Space Station if it suffers serious damage in orbit.

For most shuttle missions, the station could serve as a temporary refuge while NASA prepared another spacecraft. But Hubble travels in a different orbit, making such a maneuver impossible.

Under the contingency plan, designated **STS-400**, Endeavour would launch with a four-person crew if NASA determined Atlantis could not safely return to Earth. The two shuttles would rendezvous in orbit, and Atlantis’ astronauts would transfer to Endeavour during a series of spacewalks.

Atlantis would then be abandoned, while Endeavour carried all 11 astronauts home.

NASA officials stressed that the rescue plan was a last resort. Engineers were closely examining images of Atlantis’ heat shield, including photographs taken during launch and detailed inspections performed by the crew in orbit.

The precautions reflect lessons learned from the 2003 Columbia disaster, when that shuttle broke apart during re-entry after its heat shield was damaged at launch.

Atlantis lifted off May 11, 2009, on the fifth and final shuttle mission to service Hubble. During the flight, astronauts were scheduled to install new instruments, replace aging equipment and attempt difficult repairs intended to extend the observatory’s life for several more years.

On the ground, Endeavour remained poised at Kennedy Space Center, a visible reminder of both the mission’s risks and NASA’s determination to bring the Atlantis crew home safely.

counterfactuals.output:
For the final Hubble servicing mission, STS‑125 in May 2009, Atlantis could not use the International Space Station as an emergency refuge. Hubble’s orbit had a very different inclination, and the shuttle lacked enough propellant to reach the ISS. NASA therefore prepared a dedicated **“launch-on-need” rescue mission, STS‑400**.

### If Atlantis were damaged

After reaching orbit, Atlantis’s crew would inspect its heat shield using cameras, sensors, and the shuttle’s inspection boom. If micrometeoroid or orbital-debris damage made reentry unsafe and could not be repaired:

- The seven astronauts would power down nonessential systems to conserve oxygen, water, electricity, and carbon-dioxide-removal capacity.
- Atlantis had enough extended-duration supplies to keep them alive for roughly three weeks or more while rescue preparations were completed.
- Hubble itself would not serve as a shelter; it had no habitable space or life-support system for the astronauts.

### Endeavour’s rescue mission

**Endeavour** was kept ready on the other Kennedy Space Center launch pad with a reduced crew of four and extra equipment. It would launch as soon as practical and rendezvous with Atlantis in Hubble’s orbit.

Because two shuttles could not dock nose-to-nose, the rescue would be conducted as an EVA operation:

1. Endeavour would maneuver extremely close to Atlantis, with the two payload bays oriented toward one another.
2. A shuttle robotic arm would grapple and stabilize the other orbiter.
3. Spacewalking astronauts would install safety tethers and create a route between the vehicles.
4. Atlantis’s seven crew members would cross outside in spacesuits, assisted by the spacewalkers and tether system.
5. Endeavour would return with all **11 astronauts**—its four-person rescue crew plus Atlantis’s seven—using specially arranged additional seating and life-support provisions.

The abandoned Atlantis would then be separated and, if controllable, commanded into a destructive reentry over an unpopulated ocean area.

NASA called this a contingency plan only; Atlantis completed the Hubble mission safely, so Endeavour was never launched as STS‑400.

**Endeavour Stands Rescue Watch as Atlantis Makes Final Call on Hubble**  
*Kennedy Space Center, Fla. — May 2009*

For the final servicing mission to the Hubble Space Telescope, NASA took an extraordinary precaution: while space shuttle **Atlantis** lifted off from Launch Pad 39A, **Endeavour** stood fully assembled on neighboring Pad 39B, prepared to launch a rescue mission if Atlantis could not safely return to Earth.

The arrangement reflected the unusual risks of the Hubble flight, designated **STS-125**. Unlike most late-era shuttle missions, Atlantis was not traveling to the International Space Station. Hubble circles Earth in an orbit inclined about 28.5 degrees to the equator, while the station flies at 51.6 degrees. A shuttle in Hubble’s orbit did not have enough propellant to make the major orbital-plane change required to reach the station.

That meant the Atlantis crew had no orbital “safe haven.”

On station missions, astronauts could shelter aboard the orbiting complex for weeks or months if their shuttle suffered serious heat-shield damage. Another orbiter could then be prepared to bring them home. For STS-125, however, NASA had to have the rescue vehicle ready before Atlantis left Earth.

### A second shuttle for a worst-case emergency

Endeavour’s contingency flight was designated **STS-400**, a “launch-on-need” mission. Its four-person rescue crew consisted of commander **Chris Ferguson**, pilot **Eric Boe**, and mission specialists **Stephen Bowen** and **Shane Kimbrough**.

If inspections showed that Atlantis had sustained irreparable damage during launch—particularly to the reinforced-carbon-carbon panels on the wing leading edges or to the thermal-protection tiles—mission managers could order the crew to conserve electricity, oxygen and other supplies while Endeavour prepared to launch.

Endeavour would then rendezvous with Atlantis in orbit. Because the two shuttles were not designed to dock with one another, astronauts would have carried out a carefully choreographed series of spacewalks and transfers between the two vehicles. Endeavour would return with all 11 astronauts: its own four crew members and the seven from Atlantis. The damaged Atlantis would be left uncrewed and later disposed of in a controlled manner.

NASA estimated that Atlantis could stretch its consumables to roughly three weeks under emergency power-conservation procedures. That limited survival window made it impossible to wait until after a problem occurred to begin assembling another shuttle. Endeavour had to be stacked, checked out and positioned on a launch pad in advance.

### Why NASA could not simply use one pad

The space agency normally preferred to process one shuttle launch at a time during the program’s final years. But Atlantis could not occupy Pad 39A and still have Endeavour ready to depart quickly enough. NASA therefore rolled Endeavour to Pad 39B, creating the striking sight of two flight-ready shuttle stacks standing side by side at Kennedy Space Center.

Pad 39B’s availability was particularly valuable because the complex was already entering a period of transition. NASA was beginning to adapt the pad for the Constellation program and the planned Ares I-X test flight. Endeavour’s rescue assignment became the final space-shuttle deployment to Pad 39B.

The dual-pad setup required separate teams to maintain both orbiters, their external tanks and solid rocket boosters, while also protecting the ability to support a rapid STS-400 countdown. Endeavour was not merely parked as a symbolic backup; it was maintained in a condition that would allow NASA to launch within Atlantis’s remaining on-orbit lifetime.

### Hubble’s value justified the added precautions

NASA accepted the complex rescue posture because the STS-125 mission was considered essential to Hubble’s future. Atlantis’s crew was assigned to install the **Wide Field Camera 3** and **Cosmic Origins Spectrograph**, replace gyroscopes and batteries, repair two instruments never intended to be serviced in orbit, and add a docking mechanism that could assist with Hubble’s eventual disposal.

The mission was also unusually demanding. Five spacewalks were planned, and the astronauts had to work with aging hardware, stubborn fasteners and delicate scientific instruments. Atlantis was flying in a region where the crew could not retreat to the station and where orbital debris remained a concern.

NASA had delayed the mission in 2008 after a failure in Hubble’s science-data handling system, using the additional time to prepare a replacement unit. The delay also gave engineers more time to refine rescue plans and coordinate the use of both launch pads.

### Endeavour released after Atlantis was cleared

Atlantis launched from Pad 39A on **May 11, 2009**. During the mission, the crew used cameras and the shuttle’s robotic arm to inspect the orbiter’s heat shield. Imagery from launch and orbital inspections was transmitted to specialists on the ground, who examined the tiles and wing-leading-edge panels for damage.

Once NASA determined that Atlantis was safe for reentry, the need for STS-400 disappeared. Endeavour was subsequently moved from Pad 39B to Pad 39A and prepared for its scheduled mission, **STS-127**, to the International Space Station.

Atlantis completed the Hubble servicing work and landed at Edwards Air Force Base in California on **May 24, 2009**, after weather prevented a landing in Florida. The mission left Hubble with new instruments and extended capabilities that would support years of additional astronomical discoveries.

Endeavour never had to launch to the rescue. Its presence on the second pad, however, was central to NASA’s decision to send Atlantis to an orbit from which the International Space Station could offer no refuge. The two-shuttle arrangement served as a visible reminder that the final visit to Hubble combined major scientific rewards with one of the shuttle program’s most elaborate contingency plans.

counterfactuals.output:
The mission was **STS-400**, the “launch-on-need” rescue plan for **Atlantis’s STS-125 Hubble Space Telescope servicing flight** in May 2009.

After the Columbia accident, shuttle flights were required to have a rescue option if inspection found heat-shield damage that made reentry unsafe. Most crews could wait aboard the International Space Station, but Atlantis’s Hubble orbit could not reach the ISS. NASA therefore prepared **Endeavour** on the second launch pad for a rapid rescue.

The plan was:

- Atlantis’s seven astronauts would power down nonessential systems and conserve consumables, giving rescuers roughly three weeks to launch.
- Endeavour would fly with only four astronauts—commander **Chris Ferguson**, pilot **Eric Boe**, and mission specialists **Stephen Bowen** and **Shane Kimbrough**—leaving capacity for all seven refugees.
- Endeavour would rendezvous with Atlantis in orbit. Because orbiters had no shuttle-to-shuttle docking system, they would hold position payload-bay-to-payload-bay and use their robotic arms to create a stabilized connection.
- Over **three spacewalks**, the STS-125 crew, spacesuits, and essential equipment would be moved between the vehicles. Endeavour would then carry an unprecedented **11 people** home.
- The abandoned Atlantis would be separated and commanded into a controlled destructive reentry over a remote area of the Pacific Ocean, rather than risk an uncontrolled breakup over land.

Endeavour remained ready on Launch Pad 39B while Atlantis flew. Atlantis suffered no unrepairable damage, so STS-400 was never launched and Endeavour was released for its next scheduled mission. It was the most fully developed shuttle-on-shuttle rescue scenario of the post-Columbia era.

## Atlantis’s High-Stakes Hubble Mission—and NASA’s Rescue Plan

When space shuttle *Atlantis* lifted off on STS-125, the final servicing mission to the Hubble Space Telescope, its seven astronauts accepted a risk most shuttle crews did not face: if their spacecraft suffered serious heat-shield damage, they could not seek refuge aboard the International Space Station.

Hubble orbits at a different inclination from the station, making an emergency rendezvous impractical. The telescope’s roughly 350-mile-high orbit also exposed *Atlantis* to a greater concentration of orbital debris. Lead flight director Tony Ceccacci described the danger plainly: “It’s definitely not a benign environment.”

The mission nevertheless promised an extraordinary scientific return. Commander Scott Altman and his crew would replace failed equipment, install new instruments and extend Hubble’s working life. Altman acknowledged the unusual stakes while emphasizing NASA’s preparations. “We understand the risks,” he said. “We’ve done everything we can to mitigate them.”

Those precautions included detailed inspections of *Atlantis*’s thermal protection system and repair techniques that astronauts could use in orbit. But NASA also prepared for the possibility that the shuttle might be too badly damaged to survive reentry.

### Endeavour on standby

For that contingency, NASA readied *Endeavour* for STS-400, a rescue flight that could launch with only four astronauts. While *Atlantis* was at Hubble, *Endeavour* waited on the second launch pad at Kennedy Space Center—an exceptional sight that underscored the mission’s risk.

Christopher Ferguson, designated commander of the rescue crew, characterized the assignment as one everyone hoped would remain only a plan. “It’s a mission we don’t want to fly,” he said.

If required, *Endeavour* would rendezvous with the disabled *Atlantis*. The two orbiters could not dock directly, so they would have been positioned close together and linked through their robotic arms. Spacewalking astronauts would then transfer the stranded crew from one shuttle to the other.

John Grunsfeld, Hubble’s veteran spacewalker and one of the most experienced astronauts aboard *Atlantis*, was expected to play a central role. Under the rescue plan, he would be among the first astronauts to cross between the vehicles, helping establish the transfer route and assisting crewmates—particularly those less experienced in spacewalking—as they moved to *Endeavour*. Spacesuits also would have been transferred because *Endeavour* could not carry enough launch-and-entry suits for all 11 astronauts before liftoff.

The operation would have been delicate. The shuttles would need to hold their relative positions without colliding, while astronauts crossed open space carrying equipment and working along tethers. *Atlantis*, once abandoned, would eventually be commanded toward a destructive reentry over a remote ocean area.

Altman captured the relationship between the two crews in a remark to the rescuers: “We’re not going to need you, but we’re glad you’re there.”

NASA never had to activate STS-400. Inspections showed that *Atlantis* was safe, and the shuttle returned to Earth after a successful mission that restored Hubble and helped keep it scientifically productive for years. Yet the waiting *Endeavour* and the carefully rehearsed rescue choreography revealed how NASA approached STS-125: pursue one of its most valuable scientific objectives, but prepare for a failure that would leave no station, no conventional safe haven and no easy way home.
